read.title: Two problems, one theorem
text: Differentiation finds slopes; integration finds accumulated area. For centuries these looked like separate problems. The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus shows they are inverse processes.

Define an accumulation function g(x) = ∫ₐˣ f(t) dt, the area under f from a up to x. If you nudge x a little to the right, the area grows by a thin strip whose height is about f(x). So the rate at which the area grows is f(x) itself: g′(x) = f(x). That is Part 1. It says that every continuous function has an antiderivative, namely its own accumulation function.

Part 2 turns this into a computing tool. If F is any antiderivative of f, then ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a). Instead of summing infinitely many rectangles, you evaluate an antiderivative at two points. For example, x³/3 is an antiderivative of x², so ∫₀¹ x² dx = 1/3 − 0 = 1/3.

Read physically, Part 2 is the Net Change Theorem: integrating a rate gives the total change. Integrating velocity over a time interval gives displacement, the change in position. To get total distance traveled instead, integrate speed, |v(t)|, so that backward motion is not subtracted.

q.q: Why does g(x) = ∫ₐˣ f(t) dt have derivative f(x)?
o: A small step adds a strip of height about f(x)
Integrals and derivatives are always equal

q.q: How does Part 2 evaluate ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx?
o: F(b) − F(a) for any antiderivative F
